fields.v: Liu, K., Pan, Y., Du, Y., Zhang, L., He, D., Xiang, Y. (2026). ProjectEvalPlus: An Agentic Software Engineering Benchmark with Automatic Language Extension and User Simulated Evaluation. ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology 35(11), Article 367, 19 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3817119
2026 (TOSEM, November 2026; received 1 Nov 2025, accepted 12 May 2026)
Journal — ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM) 35(11), Article 367, November 2026, DOI 10.1145/3817119; extends the authors' ProjectEval (Findings of ACL 2025)
Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, China (Liu, Du, Zhang, He); Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China (Liu, Pan, Du, Xiang)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — ProjectEvalPlus, a project-level benchmark (20 missions, three input levels, user-interaction-simulation tests, Automatic Language Extension (ALE) to Python, Java, JavaScript), used to compare 18 LLMs ('LLM agents') in Cascade vs E2E generation modes and across languages, and ALE translation with 5 models

No SDD approach. Evaluated 'LLM agents' are models: closed-source GPT-5, GPT-3.5-turbo, Gemini 2.5-flash; open-source general Gemma-3-12B/27B, GPT-oss-20B, Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.3-70B, Phi4-14B, Qwen3-14B/30B; coding models CodeLlama-13B/34B/70B, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B/33B, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B/32B; ALE with GPT-5-mini, Gemini-2.5-flash, Gemma3-27B, GPT-oss-20B, Qwen3-30B. Two generation modes defined by the benchmark: Cascade (checklist, then skeleton, then code) and E2E (code directly). Agent scaffolding and model snapshots not stated

N/A (no approach). Benchmark inputs per mission: Level 1 natural-language prompt, Level 2 natural-language checklist, Level 3 code skeleton with docstrings; agent outputs code (JSON format) and Parameter Values (PV) answering the Parameter Descriptions (PD); Cascade mode produces intermediate checklist and skeleton

Cascade: Level 1 → checklist → skeleton → code; Level 2 → skeleton → code. E2E: code directly from the input (Level 3 only E2E). Evaluation: generate code → same agent answers PDs with PVs → project built in sandbox → user-simulation testcodes run. Parts mapped to personas: project manager (checklist), architect (skeleton), programmer (code), test engineer (PV)

None during evaluation (automatic, 'without human intervention'). Human review only in benchmark construction: refinement of Level 2 checklists, correction of canonical code, minor manual corrections after ALE
N/A (no SDD approach); project generation from three input levels in Cascade and E2E modes; ALE iterative translation with test feedback
Not classifiable (no SDD; authors do not use SDD terms; Level 2 checklist and Level 3 skeleton act as given specifications of increasing detail)
New project (whole project generated from prompt, checklist or skeleton); plus translation of the existing Python canonical code to Java/JavaScript (ALE)

20 missions (7 from SoftwareDev/ProjectDev, 13 by the authors), 284 test points (average 14.2 per mission), 16 full-stack web missions; difficulty easy/medium/hard/human; 3 languages; project size in LOC not stated
Small applications: web sites (e.g., checklist/todo application) and console/batch programs (e.g., Excel file output); Python, Java, JavaScript
N/A (no human participants; fully automatic evaluation)
None (Pass@5 dropped 'to save computing resources'; no tokens, time or money reported)
Pass@1 = percentage of test points passed (user-interaction simulation; cascaded test points); ALE: test-point pass rate before and after feedback iterations
None
None

'Objective indicators': checklist semantic similarity (Sentence Transformer + Jonker-Volgenant), skeleton and code structural similarity to canonical code (CodeBLEU + Jonker-Volgenant), PV string similarity (Levenshtein); logical and runtime error feedback per test point

Automatic: projects built and run in a sandbox; Selenium browser simulation for web missions, Python subprocess for console/batch, Openpyxl for file outputs; similarity indicators computed automatically. Temperature 0 (or minimum supported), other settings default; one run (Pass@1)

Agent scaffolding not stated for all entries; values are Pass@1 (%) averaged over three languages: Cascade L1 / Cascade L2 / E2E L1 / E2E L2 / Level 3 / Avg (Table 3). (1) GPT-5: 12.6 / 34.6 / 23.1 / 33.2 / 44.6 / 29.6. (2) Gemini 2.5-flash: 7.3 / 13.6 / 16.7 / 14.8 / 25.1 / 15.5. (3) GPT-3.5-turbo: 2.5 / 2.5 / 2.3 / 2.5 / 3.9 / 2.7. (4) Open-source general models (rebuilt from the jumbled table, see Notes): Gemma-3-12B 2.9 / 0.6 / 3.1 / 1.6 / 7.2 / 3.1; Gemma-3-27B 3.8 / 2.7 / 3.1 / 3.2 / 10.6 / 4.6; GPT-oss-20B 4.8 / 5.6 / 7.5 / 6.2 / 10.4 / 6.9; Llama3.1-8B 0.8 / 1.2 / 0.2 / 0.7 / 0.4 / 0.7; Llama3.3-70B 4.7 / 4.6 / 7.9 / 7.9 / 8.1 / 6.6; Phi4-14B 2.1 / 3.1 / 6.6 / 6.2 / 8.9 / 5.4; Qwen3-14B 2.2 / 1.9 / 2.8 / 1.6 / 3.1 / 2.3; Qwen3-30B 4.7 / 7.0 / 4.0 / 4.2 / 9.3 / 5.8 (column averages over all models 4.4 / 7.0 / 7.0 / 7.5 / 8.1). (5) Seven coding models, Level 3 E2E only: CodeLlama-13B 0.7, CodeLlama-34B 0.0, CodeLlama-70B 0.0, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B 0.9, DeepSeek-Coder-33B 2.6, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B 3.1, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B 7.5. (6) ALE translation, without → with ALE (Python→Java; Python→JavaScript): GPT-5-mini 58.0→86.2; 63.2→93.3. Gemini-2.5-flash 5.8→22.6; 22.2→60.9. GPT-oss-20B 27.4→41.8; 45.1→81.2. Gemma3-27B 16.6→19.9; 26.5→32.6. Qwen3-30B 3.9→8.8; 6.5→19.2. ALE stop rule: pass rate ≥ 0.9 or 5 iterations. Success criterion for all: test points passed; no threshold for success. Quality verdict: no criterion stated by the authors. Cost verdict: not measured

Tasks: 20 missions × 3 languages × 3 input levels. Configurations: 18 models × Cascade (L1, L2) and E2E (L1, L2, L3); coding models only Level 3; ALE: 5 models with and without ALE. Baseline: none for the model comparison (Cascade vs E2E compared with each other; ALE vs initial translation). Held constant: missions, hidden testcodes and canonical parameter values, temperature 0 (or minimum), JSON format, sandbox; agent scaffolding not described. Acceptance tests: user-simulation testcodes. Repetitions: one (Pass@1, justified by temperature 0). Human intervention: none during evaluation

GPT-5 best overall (avg 29.6; Level 3 44.6), Gemini 2.5-flash 15.5, GPT-3.5-turbo 2.7; open-source models low; coding models 0.0-7.5 at Level 3. E2E beats Cascade at Level 1 for Gemini-2.5-flash (16.7 vs 7.3) and GPT-5 (23.1 vs 12.6), and by at least 2.5 points for GPT-oss-20B, Llama-3.3-70B and Phi-4-14B; at Level 2 the E2E advantage persists only for Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen-3-30B favours Cascade (GPT-5 Cascade 34.6 vs E2E 33.2). Language: JavaScript highest overall average (9.0 vs Python 7.6, Java 5.7); Python leads among closed-source models. ALE improves all five models (+3.2 to +38.7 points). No significance tests

Distinguished models (wide spread between closed- and open-source), modes and languages. Not repeated (single Pass@1 run at temperature 0). Limitations stated: some models cannot use temperature 0 and outputs vary across hardware; cascaded test points amplify small deviations (observed once in ALE); undetectable agent 'cheating' (hard-coded outputs, mocked responses); occasional timeouts from OS, VM, browser or network; CodeBLEU indicators less accurate than Pass@1

Limitations: agent 'cheating' not detectable; environment timeouts (internet needed for packages, VM slowdowns, I/O, slow page loads); LLM instability despite temperature 0. Authors' conclusions: E2E mitigates the 'Chinese Whispers' degradation of hierarchical document handovers; language preference context-dependent. Gaps / future work: multimodal benchmark (UI vision, console output, spoken prompts); whether instability can be mitigated is an open question

Inconsistencies: in Table 3 the Avg. row gives 4.8 in the Avg. column, below every per-setting average (4.4-8.1) (p. 12); text says the Level 2 E2E advantage 'persisted only for Llama-3.3-70B', but rebuilt Table 3 also gives Phi4-14B E2E L2 6.2 vs Cascade L2 3.1 (p. 11-12); ALE gains in text/Table 6 (+16.7, +3.2) differ by 0.1 from the before/after values (16.8, 3.3), rounding (p. 14-15); Table 6 caption repeats 'Bold emphasizes the difference between ProjectEvalPlus and its peers' (p. 15); 'theoretically proves' support for all languages without a formal proof (p. 9). Table 1, Table 4 and Table 5 open-source rows are jumbled in the extracted text and not used; the Table 3 open-source rows were rebuilt by reading the numbers row by row (6 per model), checked against each row's Avg and the column Avg row. 'LLM agents' are models; no agent framework named. Repository: https://github.com/RyanLoil/ProjectEvalPlus/ (open source). Pre-registration: not claimed. Programming languages: Python, Java, JavaScript (testcodes in Python)
